summary: This government bill creates a new Proceeds of Crime Act that sets out how the state can freeze and take money and property gained from serious crimes, or used to commit them. Property can be confiscated after a conviction and, in exceptional cases such as when the suspect has died, fled or cannot be prosecuted, without one, if the Prosecutor General proves in the High Court on the civil standard that it came from crime. Before a case ends, courts can order bank accounts to be monitored, records to be handed over, accounts frozen and property restrained. A new Asset Management Office would look after seized property, and a Recovered Assets Fund would hold the money, paying victims first. The bill also sets rules for cooperating with foreign countries and repeals the asset-confiscation articles of the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act (Law 2/2015) and the Anti-Money Laundering Act (Law 10/2014).
whyItMatters: People convicted of, or in some cases only linked to, crimes such as corruption, drug trafficking, money laundering, large frauds or tax evasion could lose homes, cash, businesses and other assets, and banks would have to obey secret monitoring and freezing orders. Victims of these crimes could be paid compensation from confiscated assets.
keyProvisions: Article 24 lists the offences covered, including money laundering, terrorism and its financing, drug and human trafficking, arms trafficking, counterfeiting, insider trading and market manipulation, and corruption. It also covers tax evasion of MVR 500,000 or more, and fraud, theft, breach of trust, handling stolen goods or smuggling of MVR 100,000 or more. It applies whether the crime happened in the Maldives or abroad, and before or after the law starts.

Investigators can ask a court for account monitoring orders (up to 3 months, Article 34), production orders for bank, property and business records (Articles 37-38), and account freezing orders (Articles 42-43), which can be kept secret from the account holder. Breaching these orders brings court fines of MVR 100,000 to 1 million, or MVR 200,000 to 5 million for breaching a freeze (Articles 35, 36, 41, 50).

After charges or a conviction, the Prosecutor General can seek a restraint order freezing the suspect's property, including property held by others (Articles 52-53). Breaching it carries a fine of MVR 200,000 to 5 million (Article 60). If someone is convicted and a restraint order is still in force, the restrained property passes to the state automatically after 6 months; owners or interested parties can challenge this or ask for items to be excluded in the High Court (Articles 62-66). The state can also seek a forfeiture order in the High Court (Articles 67-68).

Without a conviction, the Prosecutor General can seek civil restraint and civil forfeiture orders in the High Court when the suspect has died, fled or cannot be prosecuted (Articles 74-90). Property is not taken if the owner shows on the civil standard that it was lawfully obtained (Article 87), and appeals go to the Supreme Court (Articles 82, 90).

Owners can ask the court to release frozen money for reasonable living costs, dependants' costs, business costs and known debts, and can ask for an order to be cancelled (for example Articles 46-47, 56-57, 79-80). Rights of good-faith third parties are protected (Articles 68, 91).

The President must set up an Asset Management Office under the finance ministry within 30 days, working independently of political influence, to manage, value, record and sell seized property, mainly by public auction or tender (Articles 95-104). A Recovered Assets Fund must be set up within 60 days of the law starting, with victims' compensation first, an annual report within 4 months of each financial year and accounts under IFRS (Articles 105-112). The law takes effect 6 months after it is published in the Gazette (Article 133).
whoIsAffected: People suspected or convicted of serious crimes and their families and business partners, banks and other financial institutions, victims of crime, the Prosecutor General and police, the courts, and foreign governments seeking or returning assets.
statedReasons: The government says the bill aims to stop offenders from benefiting from crime by setting a legal framework to confiscate criminal proceeds after conviction and, in exceptional cases, without one, to freeze such property, to manage and dispose of it, and to cooperate with foreign countries on assets moved across borders.
